recorded: 11 April 1950, Columbia 30th Street Studio, New York
intro: A little serenade passes between the pianist’s hands, its tune flicked into life by grace notes. Debussy keeps the soft pedal down throughout, even when the doll’s song becomes emphatic.

sections.label: A · Grace notes and plucked chords
sections.mNote: The tune changes hands above detached accompaniment

sections.label: B · Sharper accents, wandering chords
sections.mNote: Chromatic notes disturb the E-major song

sections.label: A′ · The song over flowing quavers
sections.mNote: Grace notes return over a smoother left hand

cues.title: A tiny plucked serenade
cues.text: Detached chords make the piano sound plucked. The tune starts in the left hand, with little grace notes that flick upwards before each longer note; then the right hand takes it over. Debussy marks the whole exchange léger et gracieux — light and graceful.
cues.evidence: Debussy, Children’s Corner, Durand (1908), plate D. & F. 7188, p. 10: detached accompaniment, grace-note tune first in the left hand, then the right, and léger et gracieux. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/0d/IMSLP252526-PMLP02387-Debussy%2C_Claude-Childrens_Corner_Durand_7188_filter.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The soft pedal stays down
cues.text: Sharps and flats creep into the tune, and sudden accents interrupt its polite little phrases. The soft pedal stays down even at forte: Debussy puts that instruction in a footnote. The doll’s serenade can raise its voice without losing its veiled piano tone.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 10, footnote requiring the soft pedal throughout, including forte passages; pp. 12–14 show chromatic phrases, accents and En animant un peu. The note describes Debussy’s instruction.
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: The left hand flows
cues.text: The grace-note song returns in E major, now carried by continuous left-hand quavers. The hands trade short notes again as the piece ends. Finally the piano reaches up to a high E and leaves a whole bar of silence under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Durand score, p. 15: returning melody over quavers, detached closing figures, high E and final bar of rests with fermatas.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Chromatic notes enter the serenade
transitions.from: A · Grace notes and plucked chords
transitions.how: The piano keeps its short, detached notes while the bass moves through chromatic pitches. Debussy cancels the four-sharp signature and writes En animant un peu. The tune strays from E major; the grace notes survive, now interrupted by sharply accented chords.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 12–13: chromatic bass, cancellation of the E-major signature, En animant un peu, grace notes and sforzando chords.

transitions.title: A running bass carries the tune
transitions.to: A′ · The song over flowing quavers
transitions.how: Rising runs cross the piano and end in a sharp accent. The left hand then starts a quiet, even pattern of quavers. Above it the right hand recalls the grace-note tune in E major, with long notes where the opening accompaniment used to pluck.
transitions.evidence: Durand score, pp. 14–15: rising runs, sforzando, the left-hand quaver pattern and the return of the E-major grace-note melody.

fields.value: Technics SL1200MK5 turntable + Audio-Technica AT95e cartridge → Radio Design Labs EZ-PH1 phono preamp → Focusrite Scarlett 2i2; Internet Archive VBR MP3 access derivative

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Debussy died in 1918 and the suite was published in 1908. This is territorial term reasoning for the composition, not worldwide clearance or a claim about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — EU public-domain term basis for a phonogram published before 1963; territorial, not worldwide.
fields.note: The documented LP issue is dated 1951, establishing publication before 1963 independently of the 1950 session. Its earlier 50-year phonogram term had expired before the 1 November 2013 extension threshold. US sound-recording status is not established. No Creative Commons licence or worldwide public-domain dedication is claimed.

composer.epithet: He trusted his ear over the rules — “pleasure is the law” — and made the piano, the flute and the orchestra sound new.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
Symbolist poetry · Mussorgsky · the Javanese gamelan · Couperin and Rameau
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, on 22 August 1862. His parents were not musicians. His father fought for the Paris Commune in 1871 and went to prison for it, and there he met Charles de Sivry, whose mother, Antoinette Mauté, taught the piano and said she had been a pupil of Chopin. She took the boy on. In 1872, aged ten, he entered the Paris Conservatoire.

His teachers could not make him out. Antoine Marmontel, his piano professor, found “a charming child, a truly artistic temperament” in January 1874; the harmony teacher Émile Durand reported in June 1879 that he was “very gifted in harmony, but hopelessly unfocused”. Years later, discussing chords at the piano with his old composition teacher Ernest Guiraud around 1890, he put his position plainly: “There is no theory. You merely have to listen. Pleasure is the law.”
